doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

chapter: Free jazz, time and the Creative Music Studio
title: Beat-for-beat attention and teaching at Creative Music Studio
summary: Berger describes his training of giving each beat equal attention so bar lines vanish, and why teaching helped CMS ask what is common to all music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Yeah, of course, yeah. You have to learn what we call beat-for-beat attention. This is our training that we do with the Creative Music Studio. I call it beat-for-beat attention. That means each beat has the same attention. So you’re not going for like one — and that’s more important than the two or the four. The four is as important as the one. And if you go for each beat, all of a sudden there’s no need for a bar line. Because you are there. So once you’re there you don’t need to know it’s four or it’s five. You are present on each beat, right? So once you go there the music becomes completely open and free you know, and then you can still play 4/4, but you’re going to play it in a different way than you did before. Because if you think bars being musical parameters, they are not. They are just lines to how the conductor keeps a band together or something. They have nothing to do with the music really. When you look at scores that Bach wrote, he didn’t write within bar lines. He put bar lines, but the phrases all go over the bar lines. All of them. As a matter of fact you can only interpret Bach’s music if you ignore bar lines. That’s what Glenn Gould did, you know, in his performances. If you listen it’s just a flow. You don’t
hear bar lines. When you hear bar lines then there’s something wrong with the music. It’s not really well assimilated.
That’s interesting you say that because I know I’m the type of person that if you put on some Latin music or some world music, I’m immediately trying to figure it out.
And if I can’t I get aggravated.

Go for each beat. That’s the point. And this is why when we started the Creative Music Studio basically we accommodated ourselves by wanting to know stuff. So the best way to learn things is to teach them. Because when you teach them you need to know what you’re talking about. So you’re going to have a lot more focus on the subject than if you just think about it. And so my question was always what is coming to all the music, to every kind of music? Because once you know that and you study from that point of view rather than from a given style, then you have much more of an ability to find out who you are as a musician, what you want to play. What is it that I want to play? Maybe I just want to play a simple song, but I’m caught in jazz school and learning — so maybe I don’t even want that and what I really want is something quite different.
